entries.32d88b730f8598e8780b79d59966889977c08266: <div sID="gen16710" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="53" osisID="Isa.53" sID="Isa.53"/> <div eID="gen16710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16711" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16712" type="x-p"/> The two great things which the Spirit of Christ in the Old-Testament prophets testified beforehand were the sufferings of Christ and the glory that should follow, <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.11">1 Pet. i. 11</reference>. And that which Christ himself, when he expounded Moses and all the prophets, showed to be the drift and scope of them all was that Christ ought to suffer and then to enter into his glory, <reference osisRef="Luke.24.26-Luke.24.27">Luke xxiv. 26, 27</reference>. But nowhere in all the Old-Testament are these two so plainly and fully prophesied of as here in this chapter, out of which divers passages are quoted with application to Christ in the New-Testament. This chapter is so replenished with the unsearchable riches of Christ that it may be called rather the gospel of the evangelist Isaiah than the prophecy of the prophet Isaiah. We may observe here, I. The reproach of Christ's sufferings—the meanness of his appearance, the greatness of his grief, and the prejudices which many conceived in consequences against his doctrine, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.1-Isa.53.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. The rolling away of this reproach, and the stamping of immortal honour upon his sufferings, notwithstanding the disgrace and ignominy of them, by four considerations:—1. That therein he did his Father's will, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.4">ver. 4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.6">6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">10</reference>. 2. That thereby he made atonement for the sin of man (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.4-Isa.53.6 Isa.53.8 Isa.53.11 Isa.53.12">ver. 4-6, 8, 11, 12</reference>), for it was not for any sin of his own that he suffered, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.9">ver. 9</reference>. 3. That he bore his sufferings with an invincible and exemplary, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.7">ver. 7</reference>. 4. That he should prosper in his undertaking, and his sufferings should end in his immortal honour, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10-Isa.53.12">ver. 10-12</reference>. By mixing faith with the prophecy of this chapter we may improve our acquaintance with Jesus Christ and him crucified, with Jesus Christ and him glorified, dying for our sins and rising again for our justification.
entries.883cc90ab9b94ffe0e11c12c532bbd68261ab355: <div eID="gen16712" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16711" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Humiliation of the Messiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen16713" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Who hath believed our report? and to whom is the arm of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> revealed? <hi type="super">2</hi> For he shall grow up before him as a tender plant, and as a root out of a dry ground: he hath no form nor comeliness; and when we shall see him, <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no beauty that we should desire him. <hi type="super">3</hi> He is despised and rejected of men; a man of sorrows, and acquainted with grief: and we hid as it were <hi type="italic">our</hi> faces from him; he was despised, and we esteemed him not. <div eID="gen16713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16714" type="x-p"/> The prophet, in the close of the former chapter, had foreseen and foretold the kind reception which the gospel of Christ should find among the Gentiles, that nations and their kings should bid it welcome, that those who had not seen him should believe in him; and though they had not any prophecies among them of gospel grace, which might raise their expectations, and dispose them to entertain it, yet upon the first notice of it they should give it its due weight and consideration. Now here he foretels, with wonder, the unbelief of the Jews, notwithstanding the previous notices they had of the coming of the Messiah in the Old Testament and the opportunity they had of being personally acquainted with him. Observe here, <div eID="gen16714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16715" type="x-p"/> I. The contempt they put upon the gospel of Christ, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.1">v. 1</reference>. The unbelief of the Jews in our Saviour's time is expressly said to be the fulfilling of this word, <reference osisRef="John.12.38">John xii. 38</reference>. And it is applied likewise to the little success which the apostles' preaching met with among Jews and Gentiles, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.16">Rom. x. 16</reference>. Note, 1. Of the many that hear the report of the gospel there are few, very few, that believe it. It is reported openly and publicly, not whispered in a corner, or confined to the schools, but proclaimed to all; and it is so faithful a saying, and so well worthy of all acceptation, that one would think it should be universally received and believed. But it is quite otherwise; few believed the prophets who spoke before of Christ; when he came himself none of the rulers nor of the Pharisees followed him, and but here and there one of the common people; and, when the apostles carried this report all the world over, some in every place believed, but comparatively very few. To this day, of the many that profess to believe this report, there are few that cordially embrace it and submit to the power of it. 2. <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> people believe not the report of the gospel, because <hi type="italic">the arm of the Lord is not revealed</hi> to them; they do not discern, nor will be brought to acknowledge, that divine power which goes along with the word. The <hi type="italic">arm of the Lord is made bare</hi> (as was said, <reference osisRef="Isa.52.10">ch. lii. 10</reference>) in the miracles that were wrought to confirm Christ's doctrine, in the wonderful success of it, and its energy upon the conscience; though it is a still voice, it is a strong one; but they do not perceive this, nor do they experience in themselves that working of the Spirit which makes the word effectual. They believe not the gospel because, by rebelling against the light they had, they had forfeited the grace of God, which therefore he justly denied them and withheld from them, and for want of that they believed not. 3. This is a thing we ought to be much affected with; it is to be wondered at, and greatly lamented, and ministers may go to God and complain of it to him, as the prophet here. What a pity is it that such rich grace should be received in vain, that precious souls should perish at the pool's side, because they will not step in and be healed! <div eID="gen16715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16716" type="x-p"/> II. The contempt they put upon the person of Christ because of the meanness of his appearance, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.2-Isa.53.3">v. 2, 3</reference>. This seems to come in as a reason why they rejected his doctrine, because they were prejudiced against his person. When he was on earth many that heard him preach, and could not but approve of what they heard, would not give it any regard or entertainment, because it came from one that made so small a figure and had no external advantages to recommend him. Observe here, <div eID="gen16716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16717" type="x-p"/> 1. The low condition he submitted to, and how he abased and emptied himself. The entry he made into the world, and the character he wore in it, were no way agreeable to the ideas which the Jews had formed of the Messiah and their expectations concerning him, but quite the reverse. (1.) It was expected that his extraction would be very great and noble. He was to be the Son of David, of a family that had <hi type="italic">a name like to the names of the great men that were in the earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.7.9">2 Sam. vii. 9</reference>. But he sprang out of this royal and illustrious family when it was reduced and sunk, and Joseph, that son of David, who was his supposed father, was but a poor carpenter, perhaps a ship-carpenter, for most of his relations were fishermen. This is here meant by his being <hi type="italic">a root out of a dry ground,</hi> his being born of a mean and despicable family, in the north, in Galilee, of a family out of which, like a dry and desert ground, nothing green, nothing great, was expected, in a country of such small repute that it was thought no good thing could come out of it. His mother, being a virgin, was as dry ground, yet from her <hi type="italic">he</hi> sprang who is not only fruit, but root. The seed on the stony ground had no root; but, though Christ grew out of a dry ground, he is both <hi type="italic">the root and the offspring of David,</hi> the root of the good olive. (2.) It was expected that he should make a public entry, and come in pomp and with observation; but, instead of that, he grew up before God, not before men. God had his eye upon him, but men regarded him not: <hi type="italic">He grew up as a tender plant,</hi> silently and insensibly, and without any noise, as the corn, that tender plant, grows up, <hi type="italic">we know not how,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mark.4.27">Mark iv. 27</reference>. Christ rose as a tender plant, which, one would have thought, might easily be crushed, or might be nipped in one frosty night. The gospel of Christ, in its beginning, was as a grain of mustard-seed, so inconsiderable did it seem, <reference osisRef="Matt.13.31-Matt.13.32">Matt. xiii. 31, 32</reference>. (3.) It was expected that he should have some uncommon beauty in his face and person, which should charm the eye, attract the heart, and raise the expectations of all that saw him. But there was nothing of this kind in him; not that he was in the least deformed or misshapen, but <hi type="italic">he had no form nor comeliness,</hi> nothing extraordinary, which one might have thought to meet with in the countenance of an incarnate deity. Those who saw him could not see that there was any beauty in him <hi type="italic">that they should desire him, nothing in him more than in another beloved,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.5.9">Cant. v. 9</reference>. Moses, when he was born, was exceedingly fair, to such a degree that it was looked upon as a happy presage, <reference osisRef="Acts.7.20">Acts vii. 20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.11.23">Heb. xi. 23</reference>. David, when he was anointed, was <hi type="italic">of a beautiful countenance, and goodly to look to,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Sam.16.12">1 Sam. xvi. 12</reference>. But our Lord Jesus had nothing of that to recommend him. Or it may refer not so much to his person as to the manner of his appearing in the world, which had nothing in it of sensible glory. His gospel is preached, <hi type="italic">not with the enticing words of man's wisdom,</hi> but with all plainness, agreeable to the subject. (4.) It was expected that he should live a pleasant life, and have a full enjoyment of all the delights of the sons and daughters of men, which would have invited all sorts to him; but, on the contrary, he was <hi type="italic">a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief.</hi> It was not only his last scene that was tragical, but his whole life was so, not only mean, but miserable, <div eID="gen16717" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen16718"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16719"/>————but one continued chain<l eID="gen16719" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16720"/>Of labour, sorrow, and consuming pain.             <hi type="small-caps">Sir</hi> R. <hi type="small-caps">Blackmore</hi> .<l eID="gen16720" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen16718"/> <div sID="gen16721" type="x-p"/> Thus, being <hi type="italic">made sin for us,</hi> he underwent the sentence sin had subjected us to, that we should <hi type="italic">eat in sorrow all the days of our life</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.17">Gen. iii. 17</reference>), and thereby relaxed much of the rigour and extremity of the sentence as to us. His condition was, upon many accounts, sorrowful. He was unsettled, had not where to lay his head, lived upon alms, was opposed and menaced, and <hi type="italic">endured the contradiction of sinners against himself.</hi> His spirit was tender, and he admitted the impressions of sorrow. We never read that he laughed, but often that he wept. Lentulus, in his epistle to the Roman senate concerning Jesus, says, "<hi type="italic">he was never seen to laugh;</hi>" and so worn and macerated was he with continual grief that when he was but a little above thirty years of age he was taken to be nearly fifty, <reference osisRef="John.8.57">John viii. 57</reference>. Grief was his intimate acquaintance; for he acquainted himself with the grievances of others, and sympathized with them, and he never set his own at a distance; for in his transfiguration he talked of his own decease, and in his triumph he wept over Jerusalem. Let us look unto him and mourn. <div eID="gen16721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16722" type="x-p"/> 2. The low opinion that men had of him, upon this account. Being generally apt to judge of persons and things by the sight of the eye, and according to outward appearance, they saw no beauty in him that they should desire him. There was a great deal of true beauty in him, the beauty of holiness and the beauty of goodness, enough to render him <hi type="italic">the desire of all nations;</hi> but the far greater part of those among whom he lived, and conversed, saw none of this beauty, for it was spiritually discerned. Carnal hearts see no excellency in the Lord Jesus, nothing that should induce them to desire an acquaintance with him or interest in him. Nay, he is not only not desired, but <hi type="italic">he is despised and rejected,</hi> abandoned and abhorred, a reproach of men, an abject, one that men were shy of keeping company with and had not any esteem for, a worm and no man. He was despised as a mean man, rejected as a bad man. He was the stone which the builders refused; they would not have him to reign over them. Men, who should have had so much reason as to understand things better, so much tenderness as not to trample upon a man in misery—men whom he came to seek and save rejected him: "<hi type="italic">We hid as it were our faces from him,</hi> looked another way, and his sufferings were as nothing to us; though <hi type="italic">never sorrow was like unto his sorrow.</hi> Nay, we not only behaved as having no concern for him, but as loathing him, and having him in detestation." It may be read, <hi type="italic">He hid as it were his face from us,</hi> concealed the glory of his majesty, and drew a veil over it, and therefore <hi type="italic">he was despised and we esteemed him not,</hi> because we could not see through that veil. Christ having undertaken to make satisfaction to the justice of God for the injury man had done him in his honour by sin (and God cannot be injured except in his honour), he did it not only by divesting himself of the glories due to an incarnate deity, but by submitting himself to the disgraces due to the worst of men and malefactors; and thus by vilifying himself he glorified his Father: but this is a good reason why we should esteem him highly, and study to do him honour; let <hi type="italic">him</hi> be received by us whom men rejected.
entries.2531bca9f95729aa4ecee797b880f8556ff61990: <div eID="gen16722" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Humiliation of the Messiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen16723" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">4</hi> Surely he hath borne our griefs, and carried our sorrows: yet we did esteem him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted. <hi type="super">5</hi> But he <hi type="italic">was</hi> wounded for our transgressions, <hi type="italic">he was</hi> bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace <hi type="italic">was</hi> upon him; and with his stripes we are healed. <hi type="super">6</hi> All we like sheep have gone astray; we have turned every one to his own way; and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> hath laid on him the iniquity of us all. <hi type="super">7</hi> He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he opened not his mouth: he is brought as a lamb to the slaughter, and as a sheep before her shearers is dumb, so he openeth not his mouth. <hi type="super">8</hi> He was taken from prison and from judgment: and who shall declare his generation? for he was cut off out of the land of the living: for the transgression of my people was he stricken. <hi type="super">9</hi> And he made his grave with the wicked, and with the rich in his death; because he had done no violence, neither <hi type="italic">was any</hi> deceit in his mouth. <div eID="gen16723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16724" type="x-p"/> In these verses we have, <div eID="gen16724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16725" type="x-p"/> I. A further account of the sufferings of Christ. Much was said before, but more is said here, of the very low condition to which he abased and humbled himself, to which he became obedient even to the death of the cross. 1. He had griefs and sorrows; being acquainted with them, he kept up the acquaintance, and did not grow shy, no, not of such melancholy acquaintance. Were griefs and sorrows allotted him? He bore them, and blamed not his lot; he carried them, and did neither shrink from them, nor sink under them. The load was heavy and the way long, and yet he did not tire, but persevered to the end, till he said, <hi type="italic">It is finished.</hi> 2. He had blows and bruises; he was <hi type="italic">stricken, smitten, and afflicted.</hi> His sorrows bruised him; he felt pain and smart from them; they touched him in the most tender part, especially when God was dishonoured, and when he forsook him upon the cross. All along he was smitten with the tongue, when he was cavilled at and contradicted, put under the worst of characters, and had all manner of evil said against him. At last he was smitten with the hand, with blow after blow. 3. He had wounds and stripes. He was scourged, not under the merciful restriction of the Jewish law, which allowed not above forty stripes to be given to the worst of malefactors, but according to the usage of the Romans. And his scourging, doubtless, was the more severe because Pilate intended it as an equivalent for his crucifixion, and yet it proved a preface to it. He was wounded in his hands, and feet, and side. Though it was so ordered that not a bone of him should be broken, yet he had scarcely in any part a whole skin (how fond soever we are to sleep in one, even when we are called out to suffer for him), but from the crown of his head, which was crowned with thorns, to the soles of his feet, which were nailed to the cross, nothing appeared but wounds and bruises. 4. He was wronged and abused (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">He was oppressed,</hi> injuriously treated and hardly dealt with. That was laid to his charge which he was perfectly innocent of, that laid upon him which he did not deserve, and in both he was oppressed and injured. <hi type="italic">He was afflicted</hi> both in mind and body; being oppressed, he laid it to heart, and, though, he was patient, was not stupid under it, but mingled his tears with those of the oppressed, that have no comforter, because <hi type="italic">on the side of the oppressors there is power,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.1">Eccl. iv. 1</reference>. Oppression is a sore affliction; it has made many a wise man mad (<reference osisRef="Eccl.7.7">Eccl. vii. 7</reference>); but our Lord Jesus, though, when he was oppressed, he was afflicted, kept possession of his own soul. 5. He was judged and imprisoned, as is implied in his being <hi type="italic">taken from prison and judgment,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.8">v. 8</reference>. God having made him sin for us, he was proceeded against as a malefactor; he was apprehended and taken into custody, and made a prisoner; he was judge, accused, tried, and condemned, according to the usual forms of law: God filed a process against him, judged him in pursuance of that process, and confined him in the prison of the grave, at the door of which a stone was rolled and sealed. 6. He was <hi type="italic">cut off</hi> by an untimely death <hi type="italic">from the land of the living,</hi> though he lived a most useful life, did so many good works, and they were all such that one would be apt to think it was for some of them that they stoned him. He was stricken to death, to the grave which he made <hi type="italic">with the wicked</hi> (for he was crucified between two thieves, as if he had been the worst of the three) and yet <hi type="italic">with the rich,</hi> for he was buried in a sepulchre that belonged to Joseph, an honourable counsellor. Though he died with the wicked, and according to the common course of dealing with criminals should have been buried with them in the place where he was crucified, yet God here foretold, and Providence so ordered it, that he should make his grave with the innocent, with the rich, as a mark of distinction put between him and those that really deserved to die, even in his sufferings. <div eID="gen16725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16726" type="x-p"/> II. A full account of the meaning of his sufferings. It was a very great mystery that so excellent a person should suffer such hard things; and it is natural to ask with amazement, "How came it about? What evil had he done?" His enemies indeed looked upon him as suffering justly for his crimes; and, though they could lay nothing to his charge, they <hi type="italic">esteemed him stricken, smitten of God, and afflicted,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.4">v. 4</reference>. Because they hated him, and persecuted him, they thought that God did, that he was his enemy and fought against him; and therefore they were the more enraged against him, saying, <hi type="italic">God has forsaken him; persecute and take him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.71.11">Ps. lxxi. 11</reference>. Those that are justly smitten are smitten of God, for by him princes decree justice; and so they looked upon him to be smitten, justly put to death as a blasphemer, a deceiver, and an enemy to Cæsar. Those that saw him hanging on the cross enquired not into the merits of his cause, but took it for granted that he was guilty of every thing laid to his charge and that therefore vengeance suffered him not to live. Thus Job's friends esteemed him smitten of God, because there was something uncommon in his sufferings. It is true he was <hi type="italic">smitten of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">v. 10</reference> (or, as some read it, <hi type="italic">he was God's smitten and afflicted,</hi> the Son of God, though smitten and afflicted), but not in the sense in which they meant it; for, though he suffered all these things, <div eID="gen16726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16727" type="x-p"/> 1. He never did any thing in the least to deserve this hard usage. Whereas he was charged with perverting the nation, and sowing sedition, it was utterly false; he had <hi type="italic">done no violence,</hi> but went about doing good. And, whereas he was called <hi type="italic">that deceiver,</hi> he never deserved that character; for <hi type="italic">there was no deceit in his mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.9">v. 9</reference>), to which the apostle refers, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.22">1 Pet. ii. 22</reference>. <hi type="italic">He did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth.</hi> He never offended either in word or deed, nor could any of his enemies take up that challenge of his, <hi type="italic">Which of you convinceth me of sin?</hi> The judge that condemned owned he found no fault in him, and the centurion that executed him professed that certainly he was a righteous man. <div eID="gen16727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16728" type="x-p"/> 2. He conducted himself under his sufferings so as to make it appear that he did not suffer as an evil-doer; for, though he was <hi type="italic">oppressed and afflicted,</hi> yet he <hi type="italic">opened not his mouth</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.7">v. 7</reference>), no, not so much as to plead his own innocency, but freely offered himself to suffer and die for us, and objected nothing against it. This takes away the scandal of the cross, that he voluntarily submitted to it, for great and holy ends. By his wisdom he could have evaded the sentence, and by his power have resisted the execution; but <hi type="italic">thus it was written, and thus it behoved him to suffer. This commandment he received from his Father,</hi> and therefore he was led <hi type="italic">as a lamb to the slaughter,</hi> without any difficulty or reluctance (he is the <hi type="italic">Lamb of God</hi>); and as <hi type="italic">a sheep is dumb before the shearers,</hi> nay, before the butchers, so he <hi type="italic">opened not his mouth,</hi> which denotes not only his exemplary patience under affliction (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.9">Ps. xxxix. 9</reference>), and his meekness under reproach (<reference osisRef="Ps.38.13">Ps. xxxviii. 13</reference>), but his cheerful compliance with his Father's will. <hi type="italic">Not my will, but thine be done. Lo, I come.</hi> By this will we are sanctified, his making his own soul, his own life, an offering for our sin. <div eID="gen16728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16729" type="x-p"/> 3. It was for our good, and in our stead, that Jesus Christ suffered. This is asserted here plainly and fully, and in a very great variety of emphatical expressions. <div eID="gen16729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16730" type="x-p"/> (1.) It is certain that we are all guilty before God. We have all sinned, and have come short of the glory of God (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">All we like sheep have gone astray,</hi> one as well as another. The whole race of mankind lies under the stain of original corruption, and every particular person stands charged with many actual transgressions. We have all gone astray from God our rightful owner, alienated ourselves from him, from the ends he designed us to move towards and the way he appointed us to move in. We have gone astray like sheep, which are apt to wander, and are unapt, when they have gone astray, to find the way home again. That is our true character; we are bent to backslide from God, but altogether unable of ourselves to return to him. This is mentioned not only as our infelicity (that we go astray from the green pastures and expose ourselves to the beasts of prey), but as our iniquity. We affront God in going astray from him, for we turn aside every one to his own way, and thereby set up ourselves, and our own will, in competition with God and his will, which is the malignity of sin. Instead of walking obediently in God's way, we have turned wilfully and stubbornly to our own way, the way of our own heart, the way that our own corrupt appetites and passions lead us to. We have set up for ourselves, to be our own masters, our own carvers, to do what we will and have what we will. Some think it intimates our own evil way, in distinction from the evil way of others. Sinners have their own iniquity, their beloved sin, which does most easily beset them, their own evil way, that they are particularly fond of and bless themselves in. <div eID="gen16730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16731" type="x-p"/> (2.) Our sins are our sorrows and our griefs (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.4">v. 4</reference>), or, as it may be read, <hi type="italic">our sicknesses and our wounds:</hi> the LXX. reads it, <hi type="italic">our sins;</hi> and so the apostle, <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.24">1 Pet. ii. 24</reference>. Our original corruptions are the sickness and disease of the soul, an habitual indisposition; our actual transgressions are the wounds of the soul, which put conscience to pain, if it be not seared and senseless. Or our sins are called our <hi type="italic">griefs and sorrows</hi> because all our griefs and sorrows are owing to our sins and our sins deserve all our griefs and sorrows, even those that are most extreme and everlasting. <div eID="gen16731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16732" type="x-p"/> (3.) Our Lord Jesus was appointed and did undertake to make satisfaction for our sins and so to save us from the penal consequences of them. [1.] He was appointed to do it, by the will of his Father; for <hi type="italic">the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all.</hi> God chose him to be the Saviour of poor sinners and would have him to save them in this way, by bearing their sins and the punishment of them; not the <hi type="italic">idem—the same</hi> that we should have suffered, but the <hi type="italic">tantundem</hi>—that which was more than equivalent for the maintaining of the honour of the holiness and justice of God in the government of the world. Observe here, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> In what way we are saved from the ruin to which by sin we had become liable—by laying our sins on Christ, as the sins of the offerer were laid upon the sacrifice and those of all Israel upon the head of the scape-goat. Our sins were <hi type="italic">made to meet upon him</hi> (so the margin reads it); the sins of all that he was to save, from every place and every age, met upon him, and he was met with for them. They were made to fall upon him (so some read it) as those rushed upon him that came with swords and staves to take him. The laying of our sins upon Christ implies the taking of them off from us; we shall not fall under the curse of the law if we submit to the grace of the gospel. They were laid upon Christ when he was <hi type="italic">made sin</hi> (that is, a sin-offering) <hi type="italic">for us,</hi> and redeemed us from the curse of the law by <hi type="italic">being made a curse for us;</hi> thus he put himself into a capacity to make those easy that come to him heavily laden under the burden of sin. See <reference osisRef="Ps.40.6-Ps.40.12">Ps. xl. 6-12</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> By whom this was appointed. It was the Lord that laid our iniquities on Christ; he contrived this way of reconciliation and salvation, and he accepted of the vicarious satisfaction Christ was to make. Christ was delivered to death <hi type="italic">by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God.</hi> None but God had power to lay our sins upon Christ, both because the sin was committed against him and to him the satisfaction was to be made, and because Christ, on whom the iniquity was to be laid, was his own Son, the Son of his love, and his holy child Jesus, who himself knew no sin. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> For whom this atonement was to be made. It was <hi type="italic">the iniquity of us all</hi> that was laid on Christ; for in Christ there is a sufficiency of merit for the salvation of all, and a serious offer made of that salvation to all, which excludes none that do not exclude themselves. It intimates that this is the one only way of salvation. All that are justified are justified by having their sins laid on Jesus Christ, and, though they were ever so many, he is able to bear the weight of them all. [2.] He undertook to do it. God laid upon him our iniquity; but did he consent to it? Yes, he did; for some think that the true reading of the next words (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.7">v. 7</reference>) is, <hi type="italic">It was exacted, and he answered;</hi> divine justice demanded satisfaction for our sins, and he engaged to make the satisfaction. He became our surety, not as originally bound with us, but as bail to the action: "Upon me be the curse, my Father." And therefore, when he was seized, he stipulated with those into whose hands he surrendered himself that that should be his disciples' discharge: <hi type="italic">If you seek me, let these go their way,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.18.8">John xviii. 8</reference>. By his own voluntary undertaking he made himself responsible for our debt, and it is well for us that he was responsible. Thus <hi type="italic">he restored that which he took not away.</hi> <div eID="gen16732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16733" type="x-p"/> (4.) Having undertaken our debt, he underwent the penalty. Solomon says: <hi type="italic">He that is surety for a stranger shall smart for it.</hi> Christ, being surety for us, did smart for it. [1.] <hi type="italic">He bore our griefs and carried our sorrows,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.4">v. 4</reference>. He not only submitted to the common infirmities of human nature, and the common calamities of human life, which sin had introduced, but he underwent the extremities of grief, when he said, <hi type="italic">My soul is exceedingly sorrowful.</hi> He made the sorrows of this present time heavy to himself, that he might make them light and easy for us. Sin is the wormwood and the fall in the affliction and the misery. Christ bore our sins, and so <hi type="italic">bore our griefs,</hi> bore them off us, that we should never be pressed above measure. This is quoted (<reference osisRef="Matt.8.17">Matt. viii. 17</reference>) with application to the compassion Christ had for the sick that came to him to be cured and the power he put forth to cure them. [2.] He did this by suffering for our sins (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">He was wounded for our transgressions,</hi> to make atonement for them and to purchase for us the pardon of them. Our sins were the thorns in his head, the nails in his hands and feet, the spear in his side. Wounds and bruises were the consequences of sin, what we deserved and what we had brought upon ourselves, <reference osisRef="Isa.1.6">ch. i. 6</reference>. That these wounds and bruises, though they are painful, may not be mortal, <hi type="italic">Christ was wounded for our transgressions,</hi> was tormented or pained (the word is used for the pains of a woman in travail) for our revolts and rebellions. <hi type="italic">He was bruised,</hi> or crushed, <hi type="italic">for our iniquities;</hi> they were the procuring cause of his death. To the same purport is <reference osisRef="Isa.53.8">v. 8</reference>, <hi type="italic">for the transgression of my people was he smitten, the stroke</hi> was <hi type="italic">upon him</hi> that should have been upon us; and so some read it, <hi type="italic">He was cut off for the iniquity of my people, unto whom the stroke belonged,</hi> or <hi type="italic">was due. He was delivered</hi> to death <hi type="italic">for our offences,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.4.25">Rom. iv. 25</reference>. Hence it is said to be <hi type="italic">according to the scriptures,</hi> according to this scripture, that Christ <hi type="italic">died for our sins,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.3">1 Cor. xv. 3</reference>. Some read this, <hi type="italic">by the transgressions of my people;</hi> that is, by the wicked hands of the Jews, who were, in profession, God's people, he was stricken, was crucified and slain, <reference osisRef="Acts.2.23">Acts ii. 23</reference>. But, doubtless, we are to take it in the former sense, which is abundantly confirmed by the angel's prediction of the Messiah's undertaking, solemnly delivered to Daniel, that he shall <hi type="italic">finish transgression, make an end of sin, and make reconciliation for iniquity,</hi> <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">Dan. ix. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen16733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16734" type="x-p"/> (5.) The consequence of this to us is our peace and healing, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.5">v. 5</reference>. [1.] Hereby we have peace: <hi type="italic">The chastisement of our peace was upon him;</hi> he, by submitting to these chastisements, slew the enmity, and settled an amity, between God and man; he <hi type="italic">made peace by the blood of his cross.</hi> Whereas by sin we had become odious to God's holiness and obnoxious to his justice, through Christ God is reconciled to us, and not only forgives our sins and saves us from ruin, but takes us into friendship and fellowship with himself, and thereby <hi type="italic">peace</hi> (that is, all good) <hi type="italic">comes unto us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Col.1.20">Col. i. 20</reference>. <hi type="italic">He is our peace,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eph.2.14">Eph. ii. 14</reference>. Christ was in pain that we might be at ease; he gave satisfaction to the justice of God that we might have satisfaction in our own minds, might be of good cheer, knowing that through him our sins are forgiven us. [2.] Hereby we have healing; for <hi type="italic">by his stripes we are healed.</hi> Sin is not only a crime, for which we were condemned to die and which Christ purchased for us the pardon of, but it is a disease, which tends directly to the death of our souls and which Christ provided for the cure of. By his stripes (that is, the sufferings he underwent) he purchased for us the Spirit and grace of God to mortify our corruptions, which are the distempers of our souls, and to put our souls in a good state of health, that they may be fit to serve God and prepared to enjoy him. And by the doctrine of Christ's cross, and the powerful arguments it furnishes us with against sin, the dominion of sin is broken in us and we are fortified against that which feeds the disease. <div eID="gen16734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16735" type="x-p"/> (6.) The consequence of this to Christ was his resurrection and advancement to perpetual honour. This makes the offence of the cross perfectly to cease; he yielded himself to die as a sacrifice, as a lamb, and, to make it evident that the sacrifice he offered of himself was accepted, we are told here, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.8">v. 8</reference>, [1.] That he was discharged: <hi type="italic">He was taken from prison and from judgment;</hi> whereas he was imprisoned in the grave under a judicial process, lay there under an arrest for our debt, and judgment seemed to be given against him, he was by an express order from heaven taken out of the prison of the grave, an angel was sent on purpose to roll away the stone and set him at liberty, by which the judgment given against him was reversed and taken off; this redounds not only to his honour, but to our comfort; for, being <hi type="italic">delivered for our offences,</hi> he was <hi type="italic">raised again for our justification.</hi> That discharge of the bail amounted to a release of the debt. [2.] That he was preferred: <hi type="italic">Who shall declare his generation?</hi> his <hi type="italic">age,</hi> or <hi type="italic">continuance</hi> (so the word signifies), the time of his life? He rose <hi type="italic">to die no more; death had no more dominion over him.</hi> He that <hi type="italic">was dead is alive,</hi> and <hi type="italic">lives for evermore;</hi> and who can describe that immortality to which he rose, or number the years and ages of it? And he is advanced to this eternal life because for the transgression of his people he became obedient to death. We may take it as denoting the time of his usefulness, as David is said to <hi type="italic">serve his generation,</hi> and so to answer the end of living. Who can declare how great a blessing Christ by his death and resurrection will be to the world? Some by <hi type="italic">his generation</hi> understand his spiritual seed: Who can count the vast numbers of converts that shall by the gospel be begotten to him, like the dew of the morning? <div eID="gen16735" type="x-p"/> <lg sID="gen16736"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16737"/>When thus exalted he shall live to see<l eID="gen16737" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16738"/>A numberless believing progeny<l eID="gen16738" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16739"/>Of his adopted sons; the godlike race<l eID="gen16739" level="1"/> <l level="1" sID="gen16740"/>Exceed the stars that heav'n's high arches grace.             <hi type="small-caps">Sir</hi> R. <hi type="small-caps">Blackmore</hi> .<l eID="gen16740" level="1"/> <lg eID="gen16736"/> <div sID="gen16741" type="x-p"/> Of this generation of his let us pray, as Moses did for Israel, <hi type="italic">The Lord God of our fathers make them a thousand times so many more as they are, and bless them as he has promised them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.1.11">Deut. i. 11</reference>.
entries.021b1a746f476b525c4d2b4447e6bdb3f44e17f2: <div eID="gen16741" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Exaltation of the Messiah; The Triumph of the Messiah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 706.)</title> <div sID="gen16742" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Yet it pleased the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> to bruise him; he hath put <hi type="italic">him</hi> to grief: when thou shalt make his soul an offering for sin, he shall see <hi type="italic">his</hi> seed, he shall prolong <hi type="italic">his</hi> days, and the pleasure of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall prosper in his hand. <hi type="super">11</hi> He shall see of the travail of his soul, <hi type="italic">and</hi> shall be satisfied: by his knowledge shall my righteous servant justify many; for he shall bear their iniquities. <hi type="super">12</hi> Therefore will I divide him <hi type="italic">a portion</hi> with the great, and he shall divide the spoil with the strong; because he hath poured out his soul unto death: and he was numbered with the transgressors; and he bare the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors. <div eID="gen16742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16743" type="x-p"/> In the <reference osisRef="Isa.53.19">foregoing verses</reference> the prophet had testified very particularly of the sufferings of Christ, yet mixing some hints of the happy issue of them; here he again mentions his sufferings, but largely foretels the glory that should follow. We may observe, in these verses, <div eID="gen16743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16744" type="x-p"/> I. The services and sufferings of Christ's state of humiliation. Come, and see how he loved us, see what he did for us. <div eID="gen16744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16745" type="x-p"/> 1. He submitted to the frowns of Heaven (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Yet it pleased the Lord to bruise him, to put him to</hi> pain, or torment, or <hi type="italic">grief.</hi> The scripture nowhere says that Christ is his sufferings underwent the wrath of God; but it says here, (1.) That the Lord bruised him, not only permitted men to bruise him, but awakened his own sword against him, <reference osisRef="Zech.13.7">Zech. xiii. 7</reference>. They esteemed him smitten of God for some very great sin of his own (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.4">v. 4</reference>); now it was true that he was smitten of God, but it was for our sin; the Lord bruised him, for he <hi type="italic">did not spare him, but delivered him up for us all,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.8.32">Rom. viii. 32</reference>. He it was that put the bitter cup into his hand, and obliged him to drink it (<reference osisRef="John.18.11">John xviii. 11</reference>), having laid upon him our iniquity. He it was that made him sin and a curse for us, and turned to ashes all his burnt-offering, in token of the acceptance of it, <reference osisRef="Ps.20.3">Ps. xx. 3</reference>. (2.) That he bruised him so as to put him to grief. Christ accommodated himself to this dispensation, and received the impressions of grief from his Father's delivering him up; and he was troubled to such a degree that it put him into an agony, and he began to be amazed and very heavy. (3.) It pleased the Lord to do this. He determined to do it; it was the result of an eternal counsel; and he delighted in it, as it was an effectual method for the salvation of man and the securing and advancing of the honour of God. <div eID="gen16745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16746" type="x-p"/> 2. He substituted himself in the room of sinners, as a sacrifice. He <hi type="italic">made his soul an offering for sin;</hi> he himself explains this (<reference osisRef="Matt.20.28">Matt. xx. 28</reference>), that <hi type="italic">he came to give his life a ransom for many.</hi> When men brought bulls and goats as sacrifices for sin they made them offerings, for they had an interest in them, God having put them under the feet of man. But Christ made himself an offering; it was his own act and deed. We could not put him in our stead, but he put himself, and said, <hi type="italic">Father, into thy hands I commit my spirit,</hi> in a higher sense than David said, or could say it. "Father, <hi type="italic">I commit my soul to thee,</hi> I deposit it in thy hands, as the life of a sacrifice and the price of pardons." Thus he shall bear the iniquities of the many that he designed to justify (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">v. 11</reference>), shall take away the sin of the world by taking it upon himself, <reference osisRef="John.1.29">John i. 29</reference>. This mentioned again (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">He bore the sin of many,</hi> who, if they had borne it themselves, would have been sunk by it to the lowest hell. See how this dwelt upon; for, whenever we think of the sufferings of Christ, we must see him in them bearing our sin. <div eID="gen16746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16747" type="x-p"/> 3. He subjected himself to that which to us is the wages of sin (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">He has poured out his soul unto death,</hi> poured it out as water, so little account did he make of it, when the laying of it down was the appointed means of our redemption and salvation. He <hi type="italic">loved not his life unto the death,</hi> and his followers, the martyrs, did likewise, <reference osisRef="Rev.12.11">Rev. xii. 11</reference>. Or, rather, he poured it out as a drink-offering, to make his sacrifice complete, poured it out as wine, that his blood might be drink indeed, as his flesh is meat indeed to all believers. There was not only a colliquation of his body in his sufferings (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.14">Ps. xxii. 14</reference>, <hi type="italic">I am poured out like water</hi>), but a surrender of his spirit; he poured out that, even unto death, though he is the Lord of life. <div eID="gen16747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16748" type="x-p"/> 4. He suffered himself to be ranked with sinners, and yet offered himself to be an intercessor for sinners, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">v. 12</reference>. (1.) It was a great aggravation of his sufferings that he was <hi type="italic">numbered with transgressors,</hi> that he was not only condemned as a malefactor, but executed in company with two notorious malefactors, and he in the midst, as if he had been the worst of the three, in which circumstance of his suffering, the evangelist tells us, this prophecy was fulfilled, <reference osisRef="Mark.15.27-Mark.15.28">Mark xv. 27, 28</reference>. Nay, the vilest malefactor of all, Barabbas, who was a traitor, a thief, and a murderer, was put in election with him for the favour of the people, and carried it; for they would not have Jesus released, but Barabbas. In his whole life he was numbered among the transgressors; for he was called and accounted a sabbath-breaker, a drunkard, and a friend to publicans and sinners. (2.) It was a great commendation of his sufferings, and redounded very much to his honour, that in his sufferings he <hi type="italic">made intercession for the transgressors,</hi> for those that reviled and crucified him; for he prayed, <hi type="italic">Father, forgive them,</hi> thereby showing, not only that he forgave them, but that he was now doing that upon which their forgiveness, and the forgiveness of all other transgressors, were to be founded. That prayer was the language of his blood, crying, not for vengeance, but for mercy, and therein it speaks better things than that of Abel, even for those who with wicked hands shed it. <div eID="gen16748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16749" type="x-p"/> II. The grace and glories of his state of exaltation; and the graces he confers on us are not the least of the glories conferred on him. These are secured to him by the covenant of redemption, which <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10-Isa.53.12">these verses</reference> give us some idea of. He promises to make his soul an offering for sin, consents that the Father shall deliver him up, and undertakes to bear the sin of many, in consideration of which the Father promises to glorify him, not only with the glory he had, as God, before the world was (<reference osisRef="John.17.5">John xvii. 5</reference>), but with the glories of the Mediator. <div eID="gen16749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16750" type="x-p"/> 1. He shall have the glory of an everlasting Father. Under this title he was <hi type="italic">brought into the world</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.6">ch. ix. 6</reference>), and he shall not fail to answer the title when he goes out of the world. This was the promise made to Abraham (who herein was a type of Christ), that he should be <hi type="italic">the father of many nations</hi> and so be <hi type="italic">the heir of the world,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.4.13">Rom. iv. 13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.4.17">17</reference>. As he was the root of the Jewish church, and the covenant was made with him and his seed, so is Christ of the universal church and with him and his spiritual seed is the covenant of grace made, which is grounded upon and grafted in the covenant of redemption, which here we have some of the glorious promises of. It is promised, <div eID="gen16750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16751" type="x-p"/> (1.) That the Redeemer shall have a seed to serve him and to bear up his name, <reference osisRef="Ps.22.30">Ps. xxii. 30</reference>. True believers are the seed of Christ; the Father gave them to him to be so, <reference osisRef="John.17.6">John xvii. 6</reference>. He died to purchase and purify them to himself, fell to the ground as a corn of wheat, that he might <hi type="italic">bring forth much fruit,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.12.24">John xii. 24</reference>. The word, that incorruptible see, of which they are born again, is his word; the Spirit, the great author of their regeneration, is his Spirit; and it is his image that is impressed upon them. <div eID="gen16751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16752" type="x-p"/> (2.) That he shall live to see his seed. Christ's children have a living Father, and because he lives they shall live also, for he is their life. Though he died, he rose again, and left not his children orphans, but took effectual care to secure to them the spirit, the blessing, and the inheritance of sons. He shall see a great increase of them; the word is plural, <hi type="italic">He shall see his seeds,</hi> multitudes of them, so many that they cannot be numbered. <div eID="gen16752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16753" type="x-p"/> (3.) That he shall himself continue to take care of the affairs of this numerous family: <hi type="italic">He shall prolong his days.</hi> Many, when they see their seed, their seed's seed, wish to depart in peace; but Christ will not commit the care of his family to any other, no, he shall himself live long, and <hi type="italic">of the increase of his government and peace there shall be no end,</hi> for he ever lives. Some refer it to believers: <hi type="italic">He shall see a seed that shall prolong its days,</hi> agreeing with <reference osisRef="Ps.89.29">Ps. lxxxix. 29</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.89.36">36</reference>, <hi type="italic">His seed shall endure for ever.</hi> While the world stands Christ will have a church in it, which he himself will be the life of. <div eID="gen16753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16754" type="x-p"/> (4.) That his great undertaking shall be successful and shall answer expectation: <hi type="italic">The pleasure of the Lord shall prosper in his hand.</hi> God's purposes shall take effect, and not one iota or tittle of them shall fail. Note, [1.] The work of man's redemption is in the hands of the Lord Jesus, and it is in good hands. It is well for us that it is in his, for our own hands are not sufficient for us, but he is able to save to the uttermost. It is in his hands who upholds all things. [2.] It is the good pleasure of the Lord, which denotes not only his counsel concerning it, but his complacency in it; and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> God loved him, and was well pleased in him, because he undertook to lay down his life for the sheep. [3.] It has prospered hitherto, and shall prosper, whatever obstructions or difficulties have been, or may be, in the way of it. Whatever is undertaken according to God's pleasure shall prosper, <reference osisRef="Isa.46.10">ch. xlvi. 10</reference>. Cyrus, a type of Christ, shall perform all God's pleasure (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.28">ch. xliv. 28</reference>), and therefore, no doubt, Christ shall. Christ was so perfectly well qualified for his undertaking, and prosecuted it with so much vigour, and it was from first to last so well devised, that it could not fail to prosper, to the honour of his Father and the salvation of all his seed. <div eID="gen16754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16755" type="x-p"/> (5.) That he shall himself have abundant satisfaction in it (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">He shall see of the travail of his soul, and shall be satisfied.</hi> He shall see it beforehand (so it may be understood); he shall with the prospect of his sufferings have a prospect of the fruit, and he shall be satisfied with the bargain. He shall see it when it is accomplished in the conversion and salvation of poor sinners. Note, [1.] Our Lord Jesus was in travail of soul for our redemption and salvation, in great pain, but with longing desire to be delivered, and all the pains and throes he underwent were in order to it and hastened it on. [2.] Christ does and will see the blessed fruit of the travail of his soul in the founding and building up of his church and the eternal salvation of all that were given him. He will not come short of his end in any part of his work, but will himself see that he has not laboured in vain. [3.] The salvation of souls is a great satisfaction to the Lord Jesus. He will reckon all his pains well bestowed, and himself abundantly recompensed, if the many sons be by him brought through grace to glory. Let him have this, and he has enough. God will be glorified, penitent believers will be justified, and then Christ will be satisfied. Thus, in conformity to Christ, it should be a satisfaction to us if we can do any thing to serve the interests of God's kingdom in the world. Let it always be our meat and drink, as it was Christ's, to do God's will. <div eID="gen16755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16756" type="x-p"/> 2. He shall have the glory of bringing in an everlasting righteousness; for so it was foretold concerning him, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.24">Dan. ix. 24</reference>. And here, to the same purport, <hi type="italic">By his knowledge</hi> (the knowledge of him, and faith in him) <hi type="italic">shall my righteous servant justify many;</hi> for he shall bear the sins of many, and so lay a foundation for our justification from sin. Note, (1.) The great privilege that flows to us from the death of Christ is justification from sin, our being acquitted from that guilt which alone can ruin us, and accepted into God's favour, which alone can make us happy. (2.) Christ, who purchased our justification for us, applies it to us, by his intercession made for us, his gospel preached to us, and his Spirit witnessing in us. The Son of man had power even on earth to forgive sin. (3.) There are many whom Christ justifies, not all (multitudes perish in their sins), yet many, even as many as he gave his life a ransom for, as many as the Lord our God shall call. He shall justify not here and there one that is eminent and remarkable, but those of the many, the despised multitude. (4.) It is by faith that we are justified, by our consent to Christ and the covenant of grace; in this way we are saved, because thus God is most glorified, free grace most advanced, self most abased, and our happiness most effectually secured. (5.) Faith is the knowledge of Christ, and without knowledge there can be no true faith. Christ's way of gaining the will and affections is by enlightening the understanding and bringing that unfeignedly to assent to divine truths. (6.) That knowledge of Christ, and that faith in him, by which we are justified, have reference to him both as a servant to God and as a surety for us. [1.] As one that is employed for God to pursue his designs and secure and advance the interests of his glory. "He is my righteous servant, and as such justifies men." God has authorized and appointed him to do it; it is according to God's will and for his honour that he does it. He is himself righteous, and of his righteousness have all we received. He that is himself righteous (for he could not have made atonement for our sin if he had had any sin of his own to answer for) is <hi type="italic">made of God to us righteousness, the Lord our righteousness.</hi> [2.] As one that has undertaken for us. We must know him, and believe in him, as one that bore our iniquities—saved us from sinking under the load by taking it upon himself. <div eID="gen16756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16757" type="x-p"/> 3. He shall have the glory of obtaining an incontestable victory and universal dominion, <reference osisRef="Isa.53.12">v. 12</reference>. Because he has done all these good services, <hi type="italic">therefore will I divide him a portion with the great,</hi> and, according to the will of the Father, <hi type="italic">he shall divide the spoil with the strong,</hi> as a great general, when he has driven the enemy out of the field, takes the plunder of it for himself and his army, which is both an unquestionable evidence of the victory and a recompense for all the toils and perils of the battle. Note, (1.) God the Father has engaged to reward the services and sufferings of Christ with great glory: "I will set him among the great, highly exalt him, and give him a name above every name." Great riches are also assigned to him: <hi type="italic">He shall divide the spoil,</hi> shall have abundance of graces and comforts to bestow upon all his faithful soldiers. (2.) Christ comes at his glory by conquest. He has set upon the strong man armed, dispossessed him, and divided the spoil. He has vanquished principalities and powers, sin and Satan, death and hell, the world and the flesh; these are the strong that he has disarmed and taken the spoil of. (3.) Much of the glory with which Christ is recompensed, and the spoil which he has divided, consists in the vast multitudes of willing, faithful, loyal subjects, that shall be brought in to him; for so some read it: <hi type="italic">I will give many to him, and he shall obtain many for a spoil.</hi> God will <hi type="italic">give him the heathen for his inheritance and the uttermost parts of the earth for his possession,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.2.8">Ps. ii. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">His dominion shall be from sea to sea.</hi> Many shall be wrought upon by the grace of God to give up themselves to him to be ruled, and taught, and saved by him, and hereby he shall reckon himself honoured, and enriched, and abundantly recompensed for all he did and all he suffered. (4.) What God designed for the Redeemer he shall certainly gain the possession of: "I will divide it to him," and immediately it follows, <hi type="italic">He shall divide it,</hi> notwithstanding the opposition that is given to him; for, as Christ finished the work that was given him to do, so God completed the recompence that was promised him for it; for he is both able and faithful. (5.) The spoil which God divided to Christ he divides (it is the same word), he distributes, among his followers; for, when he <hi type="italic">led captivity captive,</hi> he received gifts for men, that he might give gifts to men; for as he has told us (<reference osisRef="Acts.20.35">Acts xx. 35</reference>) he did himself reckon it more blessed and honourable to give than to receive. Christ conquered for us, and through him we are more than conquerors. He has divided the spoils, the fruits of his conquest, to all that are his: let us therefore cast in our lot among them.  <chapter eID="Isa.53"/> <div eID="gen16757" type="x-p"/>

entries.d87ccb1ca778ed2afd750eb45b8ad46ca977a753: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9338"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 53</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.53.1-Isa.53.12">Is 53:1-12</reference>. Man's Unbelief: Messiah's Vicarious Sufferings, and Final Triumph for Man.</title> <div sID="gen16051" type="x-p"/> The speaker, according to Horsley, personates the repenting Jews in the latter ages of the world coming over to the faith of the Redeemer; the whole is their penitent confession. This view suits the context (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.7-Isa.52.9">Is 52:7-9</reference>), which is not to be fully realized until Israel is restored. However, primarily, it is the abrupt exclamation of the prophet: "Who hath believed our report," that of Isaiah and the other prophets, as to Messiah? The infidel's objection from the unbelief of the Jews is anticipated and hereby answered: that unbelief and the cause of it (Messiah's humiliation, whereas they looked for One coming to reign) were foreseen and foretold.<div eID="gen16051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16052" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9338"/><hi type="bold">1. report--</hi>literally, "the thing heard," referring to which sense Paul says, "So, then, faith cometh by hearing" (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.16">Ro 10:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.10.17">17</reference>).<div eID="gen16052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16053" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">arm--</hi>power (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.10">Is 40:10</reference>); exercised in miracles and in saving men (<reference osisRef="Rom.1.16">Ro 1:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.18">1Co 1:18</reference>). The prophet, as if present during Messiah's ministry on earth, is deeply moved to see how few believed on Him (<reference osisRef="Isa.49.4">Is 49:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.6.6">Mr 6:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.9.19">9:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.1.15">Ac 1:15</reference>). Two reasons are given why all ought to have believed: (1) The "report" of the "ancient prophets." (2) "The arm of Jehovah" exhibited in Messiah while on earth. In Horsley's view, this will be the penitent confession of the Jews, "How few of our nation, in Messiah's days, believed in Him!" <div eID="gen16053" type="x-p"/>
entries.4e2548cfb74b9d69fefc2e0c8999181b1d561419: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9339"/><div sID="gen16054" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9339"/><hi type="bold">2. tender plant--</hi>Messiah grew silently and insensibly, as a sucker from an ancient stock, seemingly dead (namely, the house of David, then in a decayed state) (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.11.1">Is 11:1</reference>).<div eID="gen16054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16055" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall grow ... hath--</hi>rather, "grew up ... had."<div eID="gen16055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16056" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">before him--</hi>before Jehovah. Though unknown to the world (<reference osisRef="John.1.11">Joh 1:11</reference>), Messiah was observed by God, who ordered the most minute circumstances attending His growth.<div eID="gen16056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16057" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">root--</hi>that is, sprout from a root.<div eID="gen16057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16058" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">form--</hi>beautiful form: sorrow had marred His once beautiful form.<div eID="gen16058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16059" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and when we shall see--</hi>rather, joined with the previous words, "Nor comeliness (attractiveness) that we should look (with delight) on Him."<div eID="gen16059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16060" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there is--</hi>rather, "was." The studied reticence of the New Testament as to His form, stature, color, &c., was designed to prevent our dwelling on the bodily, rather than on His moral beauty, holiness, love, &c., also a providential protest against the making and veneration of images of Him. The letter of P. Lentulus to the emperor Tiberius, describing His person, is spurious; so also the story of His sending His portrait to Abgar, king of Edessa; and the alleged impression of His countenance on the handkerchief of Veronica. The former part of this verse refers to His birth and childhood; the latter to His first public appearance [Vitringa]. <div eID="gen16060" type="x-p"/>
entries.37f658a60935cdfcff7473d71387ed5e6be4ecd1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9340"/><div sID="gen16061" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9340"/><hi type="bold">3. rejected--</hi>"forsaken of men" [Gesenius]. "Most abject of men." Literally, "He who ceases from men," that is, is no longer regarded as a man [Hengstenberg]. (See on <reference osisRef="Isa.52.14">Is 52:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.49.7">Is 49:7</reference>).<div eID="gen16061" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16062" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">man of sorrows--</hi>that is, whose distinguishing characteristic was sorrows.<div eID="gen16062" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16063" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">acquainted with--</hi>familiar by constant contact with.<div eID="gen16063" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16064" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">grief--</hi>literally, "disease"; figuratively for all kinds of calamity (<reference osisRef="Jer.6.14">Jr 6:14</reference>); leprosy especially represented this, being a direct judgment from God. It is remarkable Jesus is not mentioned as having ever suffered under sickness.<div eID="gen16064" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16065" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and we hid ... faces--</hi>rather, as one who causes men to hide their faces from Him (in aversion) [Maurer]. Or, "He was as an hiding of the face before it," that is, as a thing before which a man covers his face in disgust [Hengstenberg]. Or, "as one before whom is the covering of the face"; before whom one covers the face in disgust [Gesenius].<div eID="gen16065" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16066" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we--</hi>the prophet identifying himself with the Jews. See Horsley's view (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.53.1">Is 53:1</reference>).<div eID="gen16066" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16067" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">esteemed ... not--</hi>negative contempt; the previous words express positive. <div eID="gen16067" type="x-p"/>
entries.87be6e282aac40380627c4a635f05e8d95f675a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9341"/><div sID="gen16068" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9341"/><hi type="bold">4. Surely ... our griefs--</hi>literally, "But yet He hath taken (or borne) our sicknesses," that is, they who despised Him because of His human infirmities ought rather to have esteemed Him on account of them; for thereby "Himself took OUR infirmities" (bodily diseases). So <reference osisRef="Matt.8.17">Mt 8:17</reference> quotes it. In the Hebrew for "borne," or took, there is probably the double notion, He took on Himself vicariously (so <reference osisRef="Isa.53.5">Is 53:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.8">6, 8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.6.12">12</reference>), and so He took away; His perfect humanity whereby He was bodily afflicted for us, and in all our afflictions (<reference osisRef="Isa.63.9">Is 63:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.4.15">He 4:15</reference>) was the ground on which He cured the sick; so that Matthew's quotation is not a mere accommodation. See Note 42 of Archbishop Magee, Atonement. The Hebrew there may mean to overwhelm with darkness; Messiah's time of darkness was temporary (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.45">Mt 27:45</reference>), answering to the bruising of His heel; Satan's is to be eternal, answering to the bruising of his head (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.50.10">Is 50:10</reference>).<div eID="gen16068" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16069" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">carried ... sorrows--</hi>The notion of substitution strictly. "Carried," namely, as a burden. "Sorrows," that is, pains of the mind; as "griefs" refer to pains of the body (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.10">Psa 32:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.38.17">38:17</reference>). <reference osisRef="Matt.8.17">Mt 8:17</reference> might seem to oppose this: "And bare our sicknesses." But he uses "sicknesses" figuratively for sins, the cause of them. Christ took on Himself all man's "infirmities;" so as to remove them; the bodily by direct miracle, grounded on His participation in human infirmities; those of the soul by His vicarious suffering, which did away with the source of both. Sin and sickness are ethically connected as cause and effect (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.24">Is 33:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.103.3">Psa 103:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.9.2">Mt 9:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.5.14">Joh 5:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jas.5.15">Jas 5:15</reference>).<div eID="gen16069" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16070" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">we did esteem him stricken--</hi>judicially [Lowth], namely, for His sins; whereas it was for ours. "We thought Him to be a leper" [Jerome, Vulgate], leprosy being the direct divine judgment for guilt (<reference osisRef="Lev.13.1-Lev.13.59">Le 13:1-59</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.12.10">Nu 12:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.12.15">15</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.26.18-2Chr.26.21">2Ch 26:18-21</reference>).<div eID="gen16070" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16071" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">smitten--</hi>by divine judgments.<div eID="gen16071" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16072" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">afflicted--</hi>for His sins; this was the point in which they so erred (<reference osisRef="Luke.23.34">Lu 23:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.3.17">Ac 3:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.8">1Co 2:8</reference>). He was, it is true, "afflicted," but not for His sins. <div eID="gen16072" type="x-p"/>
entries.47a50368594fd7277cb577a012aed3130c068a22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9342"/><div sID="gen16073" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9342"/><hi type="bold">5. wounded--</hi>a bodily wound; not mere mental sorrow; literally, "pierced"; minutely appropriate to Messiah, whose hands, feet, and side were pierced (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.16">Psa 22:16</reference>). The Margin, wrongly, from a Hebrew root, translates, "tormented."<div eID="gen16073" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16074" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for ... for--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Rom.4.25">Ro 4:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.21">2Co 5:21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.9.28">He 9:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.24">1Pe 2:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">3:18</reference>)--the cause for which He suffered not His own, but our sins.<div eID="gen16074" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16075" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">bruised--</hi>crushing inward and outward suffering (see on <reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Is 53:10</reference>).<div eID="gen16075" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16076" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">chastisement--</hi>literally, the correction inflicted by a parent on children for their good (<reference osisRef="Heb.12.5-Heb.8.10">He 12:5-8, 10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Heb.8.11">11</reference>). Not punishment strictly; for this can have place only where there is guilt, which He had not; but He took on Himself the chastisement whereby the peace (reconciliation with our Father; <reference osisRef="Rom.5.1">Ro 5:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.14">Ep 2:14</reference>, 15, 17) of the children of God was to be effected (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.14">He 2:14</reference>).<div eID="gen16076" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16077" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon him--</hi>as a burden; parallel to "hath borne" and "carried."<div eID="gen16077" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16078" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stripes--</hi>minutely prophetical of His being scourged (<reference osisRef="Matt.27.26">Mt 27:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.24">1Pe 2:24</reference>).<div eID="gen16078" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16079" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">healed--</hi>spiritually (<reference osisRef="Ps.41.4">Psa 41:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.8.22">Jr 8:22</reference>). <div eID="gen16079" type="x-p"/>
entries.ed5cda6a2126213a2aba6de0a927a22cdf97a017: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9343"/><div sID="gen16080" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9343"/>6. Penitent confession of believers and of Israel in the last days (<reference osisRef="Zech.12.10">Zec 12:10</reference>).<div eID="gen16080" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16081" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sheep ... astray--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.119.176">Psa 119:176</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.25">1Pe 2:25</reference>). The antithesis is, "In ourselves we were scattered; in Christ we are collected together; by nature we wander, driven headlong to destruction; in Christ we find the way to the gate of life" [Calvin]. True, also, literally of Israel before its coming restoration (<reference osisRef="Ezek.34.5">Eze 34:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.10.2">Zec 10:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.10.6">6</reference>; compare with <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.23">Eze 34:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.24">24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.4">Jr 23:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.23.5">5</reference>; also <reference osisRef="Matt.9.36">Mt 9:36</reference>).<div eID="gen16081" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16082" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">laid--</hi>"hath made to light on Him" [Lowth]. Rather, "hath made to rush upon Him" [Maurer].<div eID="gen16082" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16083" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the iniquity--</hi>that is, its penalty; or rather, as in <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.21">2Co 5:21</reference>; He was not merely a sin offering (which would destroy the antithesis to "righteousness"), but "sin for us"; sin itself vicariously; the representative of the aggregate sin of all mankind; not sins in the plural, for the "sin" of the world is one (<reference osisRef="Rom.5.16">Ro 5:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rom.5.17">17</reference>); thus we are made not merely righteous, but righteousness, even "the righteousness of God." The innocent was punished as if guilty, that the guilty might be rewarded as if innocent. This verse could be said of no mere martyr. <div eID="gen16083" type="x-p"/>
entries.8fb7bf22e0b6a0e06eb3e94aebd72919abf24786: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9344"/><div sID="gen16084" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9344"/><hi type="bold">7. oppressed--</hi>Lowth translates, "It was exacted, and He was made answerable." The verb means, "to have payment of a debt sternly exacted" (<reference osisRef="Deut.15.2">De 15:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.15.3">3</reference>), and so to be oppressed in general; the exaction of the full penalty for our sins in His sufferings is probably alluded to.<div eID="gen16084" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16085" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and ... afflicted--</hi>or, and yet He suffered, or bore Himself patiently, &c. [Hengstenberg and Maurer]. Lowth's translation, "He was made answerable," is hardly admitted by the Hebrew.<div eID="gen16085" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16086" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">opened not ... mouth--</hi><reference osisRef="Jer.11.19">Jr 11:19</reference>; and David in <reference osisRef="Ps.38.13">Psa 38:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.38.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.39.9">39:9</reference>, prefiguring Messiah (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.63">Mt 26:63</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.27.12">27:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.27.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.23">1Pe 2:23</reference>). <div eID="gen16086" type="x-p"/>
entries.26c8d9618496451edf40a13a08ac0f47fff78faf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9345"/><div sID="gen16087" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9345"/>8. Rather, "He was taken away (that is, cut off) by oppression and by a judicial sentence"; a hendiadys for, "by an oppressive judicial sentence" [Lowth and Hengstenberg]. Gesenius not so well, "He was delivered from oppression and punishment" only by death. English Version also translates, "from ... from," not "by ... by." But "prison" is not true of Jesus, who was not incarcerated; restraint and bonds (<reference osisRef="John.18.24">Joh 18:24</reference>) more accord with the Hebrew. <reference osisRef="Acts.8.33">Ac 8:33</reference>; translate as the Septuagint: "In His humiliation His judgment (legal trial) was taken away"; the virtual sense of the Hebrew as rendered by Lowth and sanctioned by the inspired writer of Acts; He was treated as one so mean that a fair trial was denied Him (<reference osisRef="Matt.26.59">Mt 26:59</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.14.55-Mark.14.59">Mr 14:55-59</reference>). Horsley translates, "After condemnation and judgment He was accepted."<div eID="gen16087" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16088" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who ... declare ... generation--</hi>who can set forth (the wickedness of) His generation? that is, of His contemporaries [Alford on Ac 8:33], which suits best the parallelism, "the wickedness of His generation" corresponding to "oppressive judgment." But Luther, "His length of life," that is, there shall be no end of His future days (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Is 53:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.6.9">Ro 6:9</reference>). Calvin includes the days of His Church, which is inseparable from Himself. Hengstenberg, "His posterity." He, indeed, shall be cut off, but His race shall be so numerous that none can fully declare it. Chyrsostom, &c., "His eternal sonship and miraculous incarnation."<div eID="gen16088" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16089" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cut off--</hi>implying a violent death (<reference osisRef="Dan.9.26">Da 9:26</reference>).<div eID="gen16089" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16090" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my people--</hi>Isaiah, including himself among them by the word "my" [Hengstenberg]. Rather, Jehovah speaks in the person of His prophet, "My people," by the election of grace (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.13">He 2:13</reference>).<div eID="gen16090" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16091" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">was he stricken--</hi>Hebrew, "the stroke (was laid) upon Him." Gesenius says the Hebrew means "them"; the collective body, whether of the prophets or people, to which the Jews refer the whole prophecy. But Jerome, the Syriac, and Ethiopiac versions translate it "Him"; so it is singular in some passages; <reference osisRef="Ps.11.7">Psa 11:7</reference>, His; <reference osisRef="Job.27.23">Job 27:23</reference>, Him; <reference osisRef="Isa.44.15">Is 44:15</reference>, thereto.
